Conducted on a large primary care sample, the first validation study of GAD-7 found good reliability, as well as criterion, construct, factorial, and procedural validity. Subse- quently, the psychometric properties of GAD-7 have been evaluated in different sample of patients, including other primary care samples [23, 24], psychiatric patients [25–27], people with addiction [28], pregnant woman [29, 30], and outpatients [29–31]. GAD-7 has also shown strong psychometric properties in different populations, such as general adults [32], elderly [33, 34] as well as people from different culture and countries [35–39]. In academic set- ting, validation was performed among Korean university students [40], Portuguese college stu- dents [41] and Saudi university male students [42]. In the context of Bangladesh, GAD-7 has been widely used in various studies as a screening tool for anxiety symptoms among adults and university students [11–13]. Moreover, Faisal et al. (2021) explored the psychometric properties of the Bengali version of the GAD-7; however, the main focus of the paper was to assess the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on anxiety, depressive symptoms and mental health status of university students [14]. Thus, a detailed assessment of factorial validity of GAD-7 focusing on Bangladeshi students has not been carried out yet. Regardless of adequate internal consistency and moderate to strong correlation with other comorbid disorders (depression, worry, etc.), findings regarding the factor structure of GAD-7 have not been consistent [43, 44]. DEPRESSION SCREENING IN COLLEGE STUDENTS 5 The Importance of Screening and Early Identification of Depression in College Students In the United States, more than 33.3% of first-year college students reported symptoms that are consistent with a diagnosable mental health disorder, according to the American Psychological Association (Auerbach et al., 2018). Mental health problems among college students have consistently increased over time and it poses a threat to their health and academic performance (Lipson, Lattie, & Eisenberg, 2019). Identification of mental health disorders among college students have been overlooked. Depression is the second most common mental health disorder among college students in the United States (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students are a key population for determining the economic growth and success of the nation. Thus, primary healthcare providers are the front line to early screening and identification of depression amongst college students. Problem Statement The prevalence of depression has risen in the college population in the past decade. There is an estimation of 33.3% of college students exhibiting significant symptoms of depression, generalized anxiety disorder, or suicide ideation (Oswalt et al., 2018). Depression is one of the most common mental health conditions among college students. In the United States, approximately 26% of individuals ages 18 and older live with a diagnosable mental health disorder in a given year (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students with depression can experience a decrease in physical health, negatively impact mental health, hinder relationships, impede academic endeavors, and decrease quality of life (Pedrelli, Nyer, Yeung, Zulauf, & Wilens, 2015).
